events.title: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut: Europe gets a direct sea route to Indian dyestuffs
events.summary: Vasco da Gama's fleet reached Calicut on 20 May 1498 and returned to Lisbon in 1499, opening a direct Portuguese sea route that bypassed Venetian and Levantine middlemen. No surviving invoice proves indigo was in the first cargoes, which were dominated by spices; but by 1516 Duarte Barbosa's price list for Calicut quoted 'good indigo', and later in the century Lodovico Guicciardini listed anil among the East Indian goods Antwerp received from Portugal.
events.significance: Created the maritime channel through which Asian indigo could reach northern Europe in bulk, setting up the long contest with European woad.

events.title: Toulouse's 'Pays de Cocagne' woad fortune peaks, then breaks
events.place: Toulouse (Hôtel d'Assézat), Lauragais woad triangle Albi–Toulouse–Carcassonne, France
events.summary: From the Middle Ages to the 16th century woad (pastel), sold as dried balls called cocagnes, made the Albi–Carcassonne–Toulouse triangle rich; a French heritage inventory cites exports of up to 200,000 bales of about 100 kg from Bordeaux in the 16th century. Pastel merchant Pierre d'Assézat built his Toulouse mansion between 1555 and 1562. The trade then entered crisis: the standard monograph (Caster) ends its study in 1561, and local accounts point to poor harvests (1560–61), the Wars of Religion from 1562, and growing competition from imported indigo. In the 17th century dyers began adding tropical indigo to woad vats.
events.significance: The Languedoc woad economy was the largest European interest threatened by sea-borne indigo, and its lobbying shaped French dye law for a century.

events.title: Imperial police ordinance bans the 'Teuffelsfarb' (devil's dye) — which was vitriol, not yet indigo
events.place: Frankfurt am Main (Reichsdeputationstag), Holy Roman Empire
events.summary: The Reichspolizeiordnung of 9 November 1577, drawn up at the Imperial Deputation Diet in Frankfurt, banned a 'newly invented, harmful, deceitful, corrosive' cloth dye 'called the Teuffelsfarb', explaining that dyers used vitriol and other cheap corrosive materials instead of woad. The text does not name indigo. Johann Beckmann (18th century) reports the ban was renewed in 1594 and 1603; only later legislation (Saxony 1650, the Empire 1654) extended the 'devil's dye' label to indigo.
events.significance: Primary evidence that the famous 'devil's dye' ban began as a quality rule against vitriol dyeing; the equation with indigo is a later (17th-century) step often back-dated in popular histories.

events.title: England's Elizabethan dye act targets logwood, and names woad-and-indigo as a lawful ground
events.summary: The 1580/81 'act for the abolishing of certain deceitful stuff used in the dyeing of cloths' banned logwood ('blockwood'), not indigo; a 1597 bill outlawed the logwood trade and Charles II's parliament legalised logwood again from 1 February 1661. Beckmann notes that the 1581 statute is the first mention of indigo in English law, requiring woollens dyed black to be first grounded blue 'by woad, or woad and indigo together'. Later claims (e.g., Andrew Ure, cited by Beckmann's 1846 editors) that Elizabeth banned indigo appear to conflate it with the logwood ban.
events.significance: Corrects a widely repeated claim: England's protective dye laws were aimed at logwood, while indigo was lawful as an adjunct to woad.

events.title: Crown tries to keep Indigenous workers out of indigo works — and turns to enslaved Africans
events.place: Santiago de Guatemala (Antigua Guatemala), seat of the Audiencia
events.summary: A 1549 order for the Audiencia of Guatemala barred hiring Indigenous people in textile and sugar mills, and repeated royal orders extended the ban to indigo obrajes, whose fermentation vats were notoriously deadly. A 1581 order (AGCA A1.23, leg. 1513, f. 565) stated the need to use enslaved people of African descent in indigo making because 'there are no black workers' and Indigenous people were being called in. Enforcement was weak: obraje owners continued to use Indigenous labour and paid fines and bribes.
events.significance: Indigo labor law in Guatemala tied the dye directly to the Atlantic slave trade while Indigenous communities kept dying in the obrajes.

events.title: France forbids indigo at the request of the Estates of Languedoc
events.summary: According to Johann Beckmann, 'in consequence of an urgent representation by the states of that province' (Languedoc), the use of indigo was forbidden in France in 1598, and the prohibition was repeated several times. events.significance: French woad protectionism was real, but the most dramatic version of it (a capital crime) remains undocumented.

events.title: Xiquilite obrajes spread along Central America's Pacific slope
events.place: Province of San Salvador, Audiencia de Guatemala (modern El Salvador)
events.summary: Indigo from the native Indigofera suffruticosa (xiquilite/jiquilite) was being shipped from the jurisdiction of San Salvador to Spain via Puerto Caballos (Honduras) by 1572. A count for 1600 lists about 200 indigo works (obrajes) in El Salvador, 40 in Escuintepeque, 60 in Guazapán and 60 more in San Miguel, Tecpanatitlán, Choluteca and Nicaragua — roughly 360 in all. Beckmann, writing in the 18th century, states that the first American indigo to reach Europe came from 'Guatimala'.
events.significance: Spanish Central America became the Atlantic world's first large-scale plantation indigo supplier, a century before the Caribbean and Carolina.

events.title: Ten captive Angolans sold in Guatemala for 85 quintals of indigo
events.summary: In the first half of the 17th century añil served as a medium of exchange in the Kingdom of Guatemala: slaves, houses, dowries and even tithe farms were priced in quintals of indigo. On 30 April 1624 Captain Duarte Gómez de Chávez sold ten newly arrived enslaved Africans from Angola to Sancho de Carranza y Medinilla for 85 quintals of coastal indigo, about 8.5 quintals per person, payable at Christmas 1625 and 1626. In 1621 the tithe of San Miguel and Choluteca was sold for 45 quintals of indigo.
events.significance: Shows indigo functioning as money in the same economy that imported enslaved Africans to make it.

events.title: Dutch and English companies fight over Bayana indigo near Agra
events.place: Bayana, Agra region (Mughal India; modern Rajasthan)
events.summary: In the early 17th century the Dutch (VOC) and English (EIC) East India companies bought indigo in two main Mughal markets: Sarkhej near Ahmedabad in Gujarat and Bayana near Agra, whose indigo was then prized as the best. In 1626 the VOC factor at Agra, Francisco Pelsaert, complained that Armenian merchants were 'running and racing about like hungry folk' in the indigo districts and driving up prices. Armenian buyers carried indigo overland to Persia, undercutting the Europeans' attempts at monopoly.
events.significance: Indigo was one of the first Indian commodities the chartered companies sought to control, before calicoes overtook it.

events.title: Seven VOC ships land 333,545 lb of Gujarat and Bayana indigo
events.place: Dutch Republic (VOC return fleet; Amsterdam used as reference point)
events.summary: Beckmann lists the indigo aboard seven ships arriving in Holland from the East Indies in 1631: 13,539 lb of 'Sirches' (Sarkhej) indigo, 82,734 and 66,996 lb of 'Guzerat' indigo, 50,795 lb of 'Bajano' and 59,698 lb of 'Bejana' (Bayana) indigo, and 32,251 and 27,532 lb of 'Chirches' (Sarkhej) — 333,545 lb in total, valued at 500,000 dollars. events.title: Guatemala's president bans Indigenous labor in indigo works — for one week
events.summary: On 26 June 1636 President Álvaro de Quiñones Osorio of the Audiencia of Guatemala issued Autos forbidding the use of Indigenous people in indigo obrajes, citing whole villages on the Pacific coast (including Tecoluca and Zacatecoluca in San Salvador) emptied by obraje labor, and took sworn testimony from clergy and officials. On 4 July 1636 the Real Acuerdo suspended the ban, arguing that royal revenues and convents financed by indigo would suffer. The year before, he had ordered non-Indians out of Indian towns and founded the villa of San Vicente de Austria (Lorenzana).
events.significance: A rare, documented moment when colonial authorities weighed indigo profits against Indigenous lives — and chose profits.

events.title: Saxony and the Holy Roman Empire outlaw indigo as a 'devil's dye'
events.place: Holy Roman Empire (imperial prohibition of Ferdinand III; Diet then sitting at Regensburg)
events.summary: Beckmann records that the first prohibition aimed specifically at indigo was issued by Saxony in 1650, worded so that indigo fell under the old 'devil's dye' label. In 1652 Duke Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha (a woad state) proposed to the Imperial Diet that indigo be banished from the Empire, and an imperial prohibition followed on 21 April 1654 against smuggled indigo. Nuremberg required its dyers to swear an annual oath not to use indigo, an oath Beckmann says they were still taking in his day.
events.significance: The German indigo ban proper dates from 1650–54, not 1577 — a protectionist response to Dutch-imported indigo undermining Thuringian woad.

events.title: Colbert's dye regulations admit indigo into French 'grand et bon teint' dyeing

events.significance: Marks France's shift from banning indigo to regulating it, as its own Caribbean colonies became major producers.

events.title: Père Labat describes and illustrates the French Caribbean indigoterie
events.summary: The Dominican Jean-Baptiste Labat, in the French Antilles from 1694, published his Nouveau voyage aux isles de l'Amérique in 1722; its engraving of indigo manufacture shows the three-vat works (trempoire or steeping vat, batterie or beating vat, and diablotin/reposoir) worked by enslaved Africans. Archaeology at L'Anse à la Barque in Guadeloupe shows indigo works built from the 17th century and abandoned in the 18th as Saint-Domingue overtook Guadeloupe; John Garrigus notes that Labat, visiting Saint-Domingue's south coast in 1701, treated indigo (like tobacco) as a crop that let planters accumulate capital for sugar works.
events.significance: Documents the indigo 'stage' of French Caribbean plantation development that preceded sugar and coffee.

events.title: Eliza Lucas's indigo trials at Wappoo produce a marketable dye
events.place: Wappoo plantation, Wappoo Creek, near Charleston, South Carolina (approximate)
events.summary: Left in charge of the family's Wappoo plantation when her father returned to Antigua in 1739, Eliza Lucas experimented with West Indian indigo seed; George Lucas sent Nicolas Cromwell, a dye maker from Montserrat, to build an indigo works, and in the fifth year of trials the plantation produced its own seed and a dye good enough to market. Six pounds of dye were sent to England, where a broker judged it as good as 'some of the best french'. Historians stress she was one of several experimenters (with Andrew Deveaux and others) and that enslaved people did the labor.
events.significance: The Wappoo trials helped launch Carolina's indigo boom, though the popular 'single-handed' story is overstated.

events.title: Carolina's own bounty and wartime shortages launch indigo exports: 138,300 lb in 1747
events.summary: In May 1744 the South Carolina legislature offered a bounty of one shilling (South Carolina currency) per pound on several new export crops including indigo, and cancelled it for indigo in April 1746 because output had grown so fast. King George's War (1739–48) had raised rice freight and insurance costs and cut Britain off from French West Indian indigo. Large-scale exports began in 1747, when 138,300 lb worth £16,803 sterling were shipped to England.
events.significance: The start of the annual Carolina export series that would reach over a million pounds by 1775.

events.title: Parliament pays sixpence a pound for British-colonial indigo
events.summary: Lobbied by South Carolina merchant and agent James Crokatt, Parliament in 1748 enacted a bounty, initially six pence sterling per pound, paid to British importers of American colonial indigo; it took effect in 1749. Indigo was already an 'enumerated' commodity that had to be shipped to Britain under the 1660 act, and nearly all Carolina indigo went there. The bounty was renewed by later continuance acts and lapsed in 1777 during the Revolution.
events.significance: An early example of imperial industrial policy: a subsidy to secure a strategic textile input from colonies rather than from France or Spain.

events.title: Enslaved 'indigo makers' carry Carolina's dye industry
events.summary: Planting, weeding, harvesting and the skilled steeping-and-beating that turned leaves into dye in South Carolina were done almost entirely by enslaved people of African descent; skilled 'indigo slaves' were valued because a year's crop depended on the indigo maker's judgment. Charles Woodmason estimated in 1755 that 50 acres needed 15 hands to grow and 25 'very able' hands to process, at about 50 lb of dye per acre. Whether Africans brought indigo expertise from West Africa is plausible but poorly documented for Carolina; a Louisiana parish museum credits enslaved West African dyers there.
events.significance: The export statistics are, in effect, a measure of coerced African labor and skill.

events.title: Indigo-dyed Indian 'blue goods' buy captives on the West African coast
events.place: East India House, London (order to Fort William, Calcutta, for African-market cloth)
events.summary: Indian cotton cloth dyed with indigo — 'blue goods' in English, 'guinée' in French, and types such as bafts, nicanees and 'guinea stuffs' — was a key currency for buying enslaved people from African brokers. In Anglo-African trade, Indian piece goods made up about 30% of total export value in the mid-18th century, and on 15 February 1765 the English East India Company asked Fort William to send more textiles to London for African markets. In the Senegal River region Indian cloth became a regional currency in the late 18th century, and S. M. X. Golberry, visiting West Africa in the 1780s, noted that the smell of indigo authenticated blue cloth as currency.
events.significance: Links Asian indigo dyeing directly to the Atlantic slave trade that supplied the labor for American indigo plantations.

events.title: East Florida's indigo colony at New Smyrna
events.summary: After Britain acquired Florida in 1763, indigo became East Florida's main export crop, worked largely by more than 9,000 enslaved Black laborers brought by planters from the Carolinas and Georgia. Scottish physician Andrew Turnbull recruited 1,403 Minorcan, Greek and Italian indentured colonists, who sailed from Gibraltar in April 1768 to grow indigo at New Smyrna; the colony collapsed in 1777 amid disease, drought and abuse. HSUS notes British Florida produced only 20,000–60,000 lb a year in the last five colonial years.
events.significance: An attempt to extend the bounty-driven indigo economy south, with indentured Mediterranean labor alongside slavery.

events.summary: Saint-Domingue dominated 18th-century European indigo supply. events.summary: The Continental Congress prohibited exports to Britain (rice excepted until summer 1777), so Carolina producers tried northern and French Caribbean buyers with limited success, and the parliamentary bounty created in 1748 expired in 1777. events.title: Guatemala City merchants handle 60% of Central American indigo
events.place: Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción (Guatemala City)
events.summary: Troy Floyd, using Spanish sales-tax (alcabala) accounts, gives Central American indigo production of 1,089,636 lb in 1778 and finds that 21 Guatemala City merchants exported almost 2,500,000 lb in 1778–1785, about 60% of total production. Indigo, gathered at fairs such as Apastepeque in San Salvador, was shipped by mule (one zurrón of about 212 lb per mule) and barge to the Caribbean port of Santo Tomás for Cádiz. events.place: San Vicente (de Austria), Alcaldía Mayor of San Salvador
events.summary: To break Guatemala City merchants' grip on credit and prices, Bourbon authorities under Matías de Gálvez founded a Sociedad y Montepío de cosecheros de añil in 1782, based at San Vicente, to advance credit to indigo growers, and moved the indigo fair from Guatemala City to San Vicente. Around this period about 90% of the Kingdom of Guatemala's harvest came from the province of San Salvador. Local conflicts followed, such as the 1783–84 dispute over hoarding of indigo seed ('mostazas') in Zacatecoluca.
events.significance: A Bourbon attempt at development finance for a colonial export crop, centred on today's El Salvador.

events.summary: England imported 266,000 lb of indigo from Bengal in 1786, as the East India Company and newly arrived British planters began producing indigo there with West Indian methods. events.title: Saint-Domingue counts 3,150 indigoteries — and free people of color own many
events.summary: Moreau de Saint-Méry's description of French Saint-Domingue as of 1789 counts 793 sugar works, 3,150 indigo works (indigoteries) and 3,117 coffee plantations; the Western Province alone had 1,804 indigoteries. Indigo's low capital needs made it a route to planter status for free people of color, especially in the southern peninsula; an indigo planter from the southern peninsula led their campaign for civil reform during the French Revolution. events.significance: Indigo shaped Saint-Domingue's social structure on the eve of the Haitian Revolution.

notes: DEVIL'S DYE (1577): The primary text of the Reichspolizeiordnung of 9 Nov 1577 (Frankfurt Reichsdeputationstag, title 21) bans the 'Teuffelsfarb' defined as dyeing with vitriol and other corrosive cheap materials instead of woad; it does NOT mention indigo. Beckmann (18th c.) says the ban was renewed 1594 and 1603, and that indigo was first specifically banned by Saxony in 1650 and by imperial prohibition of 21 April 1654 (proposal by Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha, 1652). Popular claims that 'Germany banned indigo as the devil's dye in 1577' (e.g., erfurt-lese.de) conflate the two. Recommend presenting 1577 as 'vitriol ban later applied to indigo'.

HENRI IV 1609 DEATH PENALTY: Repeated widely (including a BnF Gallica blog, which gives no date or source) but no primary text or archival citation was found. Beckmann, a careful 18th-century compiler who cites Hellot's 1740 Académie memoir, instead records a French prohibition of indigo in 1598 at the request of the Estates of Languedoc, repeated several times. Treat '1609 death penalty' as UNVERIFIED/probably folklore.

ENGLAND/ELIZABETH: The 1580/81 statute (23 Eliz. c. 9) and a 1597 bill banned LOGWOOD ('blockwood'), not indigo; Beckmann says the 1581 act is the first mention of indigo in English law, as a permitted ground ('woad, or woad and indigo together') before black dyeing. Andrew Ure's claim (quoted by Beckmann's 1846 editors) that Elizabeth banned indigo and ordered it burned appears to conflate indigo with logwood. Logwood was legalised from 1 Feb 1661 (Dodge 2025).

COLBERT 1669: Beckmann's English translation says the 1669 edict stated 'indigo should be used without woad', which is almost certainly a translation slip for 'not without woad' (i.e., indigo permitted only in combination). The 1671 Instruction générale standardised 13 blues. The 1737 liberalisation (indigo alone or mixed) is stated by Beckmann; the search-surfaced attribution of 1737 to controller-general Philibert Orry was not verified.

BOUNTY DATE: The Act is 21 Geo. II c. 30 (session 1747/48; 'Importation of Indigo Act 1747'); CCPL says enacted spring 1748, effective 1749; the South Carolina Encyclopedia says Parliament was persuaded 'in 1749'. HSUS (1975) misprints the citation as '21 Charles II c 30'. The bounty lapsed in 1777 (CCPL; Wikipedia's article on the Making of Indigo, etc. Act 1770 says it was continued to the end of the session after 25 March 1777 — PENDING). Reported reductions of the rate (to 4d) were NOT verified.

HSUS SERIES CAVEATS: 1775 = 6½ months ending 24 Feb (not a calendar year); 1774 = 11 months; 1773 = year ending 11 Nov; 1747-1751 = years ending 24 March; 1752 = 9½ months. 1766 and 1783-1788 are Charleston only (other ports = 7.8% in 1768-73). 1747 and 1749 both print 138.3. 1768 and 1772 exclude casks listed in footnotes. SCE's 1787 figure (907,258 lb) differs from HSUS 974.1 thousand (Charleston).

NGE (Georgia) says Carolina exported 'around 200,000 pounds' in 1755 and that the British bounty was offered 'immediately' after Eliza Lucas's 1744 sample; HSUS shows 303,500 lb in 1755 and the bounty dates to 1748-49. Prefer HSUS.

ELIZA LUCAS: CCPL (Nic Butler) argues her role 'has been greatly exaggerated'; contemporaries Andrew Deveaux, Charles Hill, Thomas Mellichamp and James de la Chappelle, plus enslaved workers, were essential. Present her as a key experimenter, not sole founder.

INDIGO AS CURRENCY IN CAROLINA: Claims that indigo circulated as money in colonial South Carolina appear only on popular sites (historyfacts.com etc.) with no primary citation; NOT included. Indigo as a documented medium of exchange is included for 17th-century Guatemala (Cabezas, citing notarial records via J. J. Falla).

WEST AFRICAN EXPERTISE: Direct documentary evidence that enslaved Africans brought indigo know-how to South Carolina is thin; CCPL calls it 'possible'. The West Baton Rouge Museum asserts it for Louisiana (Yoruba, Soninke etc.) without citing sources. Present as plausible, not proven, for Carolina.

GUATEMALA SERIES: Robert S. Smith (HAHR 1959) and J. A. Fernández Molina (Pintando el mundo de azul, 2003) contain annual Central American series; neither was accessible (403). Only period averages (via Martin 2019 and a search rendering of Díaz Arias & Viales 2016) and scattered years (Floyd 1965; AFEHC/Browning) are provided. AFEHC table labels the 1,333,185-libra harvest as 1792 but its text says 1793.

BRITISH IMPORTS BY ORIGIN c. 1770-1800 (priority 3): not found in an accessible primary table. Proxies provided: HSUS Z 294 (1770 colonial exports to GB: 584,593 lb), Bengal→England 1786 (266,000 lb) and from 1794 (1.4 million lb). A commonly repeated statement that ~30% of Britain's indigo came from India in 1788 rising to 95% by 1810 was seen only in search-engine summaries and is NOT included. Nash (2010) is the best scholarly source for British import shares (paywalled).

SAINT-DOMINGUE: The frequently cited counts '~1,000 indigoteries in 1713' and '3,160 in 1790' were seen only in search summaries; Moreau de Saint-Méry's own 1797 text gives 3,150 (c. 1789), used here. Moreau figures come from archive.org OCR (long-s); the key digits are clean. Delamare (2019) states Bordeaux received 1,800 tonnes of indigo in 1771; this looks implausibly high relative to Martin's figures and is NOT used.

VASCO DA GAMA: No evidence that indigo was in the 1499 return cargo (Beckmann explicitly could not find any invoice). The da Gama event is framed as the opening of the sea route; the BnF blog's statement that Indian indigo imports to Europe began only 'vers 1631' conflicts with Barbosa (1516) and Guicciardini (1560s) as reported by Beckmann.

BAYANA/SARKHEJ: World History Encyclopedia places both in 'northern India'; Sarkhej is near Ahmedabad (Gujarat, western India), Bayana near Agra. Coordinates used: Bayana 26.9075, 77.2902; Sarkhej 22.9887, 72.5020. EIC annual indigo import quantities (K. N. Chaudhuri 1965/1978) were not accessible.

TOULOUSE COLLAPSE: Dating the crisis to 1560-62 rests on Caster's 1962 monograph (end date 1561) and local accounts (university student blog; tourism pages) citing poor harvests, fraud, Wars of Religion and indigo competition. No accessible scholarly page was found stating the causes directly; treat causation as PENDING. Persée article texts (Brumont 1994; Cardon 2020 in Annales du Midi) were blocked.

COORDINATES: Wappoo plantation (32.764, -79.989) is approximate (Wappoo Creek west of Charleston). Saint-Domingue colony-level events use a central point (19.0, -72.3). The 1654 imperial prohibition is placed at Regensburg, where the Diet of 1653-54 sat; the exact place of issue was not verified. The Mouzon map event uses London (place of publication).
ERAS: per brief, 'searoutes' 1498-1649, 'plantation' 1650-1789, 'bengal' 1790+. Series include a few post-1800 context points (1811 Central America; 1815 Bengal) flagged in point notes.
